name: nkf
why: Network Kanji filter converts between Japanese encodings like ISO-2022-JP and Shift_JIS, a sliver of computing history worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: nkf (Network Kanji Filter) is a command-line filter that converts Japanese text between character encodings. It reads text from files or standard input and writes it out in a designated encoding such as ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32. It can also convert line endings, convert half-width and full-width kana and alphabet forms, and decode or encode MIME, base64, quoted-printable, URL, hex and HTML numeric character references. The README's own description is: "Nkf is a yet another kanji code converter among networks, hosts and terminals."
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a converter for moving Japanese text between networks, hosts and terminals that each use different kanji codes. Its distinguishing idea is that users do not have to say what the input encoding is.
brief.how_it_works: Input encoding is guessed automatically. The README says it recognizes ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32, so users needn't set the input kanji code explicitly. By default half-width (X0201) katakana is converted to full-width (X0208) kana, and for automatic detection nkf assumes there is no X0201 kana in Shift_JIS. Options such as -X, -x or -S change that assumption.

brief.install_notes: The README does not cover installation beyond the Homebrew formula named in the brief. It names no runtime, account, or first-run configuration. Some options take extra arguments (for example --ic=input codeset and --oc=output codeset, where codeset names are case insensitive), and -l cannot be combined with -s, -e or -x.
brief.standout: Automatic input-encoding detection across several Japanese encodings and Unicode forms means the caller never has to declare the source. It is a small, single-purpose filter in the Unix tradition, and the README's history (a 1987 Fujitsu original, later extended by The nkf Project) is part of its appeal.
brief.status: unknown. The README is a man-page-style document with no release date, version number, or recent-change note. The copyright line runs to 1996-2012, which suggests the text has not been revised for a long time. I did not check the commit history or releases page.
brief.caveats: Automatic detection assumes Shift_JIS input has no half-width kana unless -X, -x or -S is given. -l is incompatible with -s, -e and -x. --in-place overwrites the original files. The README says to use --no-best-fit-chars when converting strings related to paths. Windows users are pointed to Windows-31J (CP932) for Microsoft's variant. The README gives no licence name, platform list, or build instructions, and I did not see a license file.

judge.reason: Its automatic guessing across Japan’s incompatible legacy encodings—and kana-normalization quirks—makes this small filter a doorway into a strange corner of text computing.

entry.title: nkf
entry.tldr: A small Unix filter that converts Japanese text between encodings like Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, ISO-2022-JP and UTF-8, and guesses the input encoding so you never have to declare it.
entry.deeper_look:
nkf, the Network Kanji Filter, reads text from files or standard input and writes it back out in the encoding you choose: ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32. It also converts line endings, swaps half-width and full-width kana and alphabet forms, and decodes or encodes MIME, base64, quoted-printable, URL, hex and HTML numeric character references.

It exists because Japanese text was long stored in several incompatible encodings, and networks, hosts and terminals each preferred a different one. The README calls it "a yet another kanji code converter among networks, hosts and terminals." The history goes back to a 1987 Fujitsu original, later extended by The nkf Project.

The idea underneath is detection. In the README's words, "One of the most unique faculty of nkf is the guess of the input kanji encodings." It recognises ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32, "so users needn't set the input kanji code explicitly." That makes it a good way into why Japanese text has so many encodings, and why guessing among them is a real problem.

The defaults reflect that history. Half-width katakana (X0201) is converted to full-width (X0208) by default, and detection assumes Shift_JIS input has no half-width kana unless you pass -X, -x or -S.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the encoding and newline type nkf guesses for the file. Use --guess=1 to print only the encoding.
Converts katakana to hiragana and writes the result to standard output.
Lists the options, which are numerous and mostly single letters.

entry.whats_unique: It guesses the input encoding across several Japanese encodings and Unicode forms, so you only say what you want out. It is a single-purpose Unix filter with a lineage back to 1987.
entry.caveats: The README has no release date or version, and its copyright line runs only to 2012, so how actively it is maintained is unclear; --in-place also overwrites your original files.
